title: Occupational Burnout in Nurses and Corporate Employees in Małopolska region, Poland
content:
Introduction: Work is an important part of human life. However, high expectations from employers and customers as well as time pressure and chronic stress can lead to the development of burnout in employees of service professions.
Aim of the study: The aim of the study was to compare the prevalence of burnout syndrome in two occupational groups: corporate office workers and active nurses, and to assess the influence of socio-demographic factors on the level of burnout in both groups. 
Material and methods: The study was conducted in a group of 330 people, including 126 nurses (38%) and 204 corporate employees (62%). The material was collected using a standard questionnaire and the Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI). The study was conducted from 11.2018  to 10.2019 and questionnaires were obtained by email.
Results: The results of the study showed that both corporate employees and nurses suffer from occupational burnout. Both groups showed a predominance of average and high values of emotional exhaustion - nurses 66.67% ( q2= 20.5), corporate employees 73.53% (q2=31.5), and a low and average sense of self-achievement - nurses 78.57% ( q2=32.0), corporate employees 87.75% (q2=27.0). Corporate employees showed significantly higher scores of depersonalization q2=13.50 than the surveyed nurses q2=5.0. The incidence of burnout in both groups was influenced by socio-demographic factors such as having children, place of residence, education, earnings, and factors directly related to performing one’s job (having a holiday, frequency of work shifts, work system, working overtime, and overall perceived job satisfaction). 
Conclusions: Groups of service occupations, related to providing care and requiring direct interpersonal contact with clients, are at comparable risk of occupational burnout. Despite the different nature and conditions of work and the tasks performed, both corporate employees and active nurses are vulnerable to burnout. It was not confirmed that high salary could be a protective factor against occupational burnout. Moreover, in addition to individual factors, environmental factors, among others those related to working conditions, also played an important role in the development of occupational burnout syndrome.
